that I shd. have troubled you at such a time.— I am, also, rather sorry you have had the trouble & risk of sending a precious Book to
, in as much as it does not contain, you say, your own observations. And now I am sorry to say I do not know
address, so will you any time during next fortnight ask to have the Book sent or left at my Brothers 57
if more convenient: I would have gone & called at Mrs.
, but the distance is so great, & I have so much to do, & so precious little strength to do it.
I could look at Book in evenings, & would return it to you direct, or to
whichever you might direct.— (A memorandum might be enclosed with Book) But all this, I am ashamed to say is giving you trouble.
Very many thanks for fact of Black-birds nests; it is just what I wanted to know: I quite agree, also, with what you say about relation of intellect & reason. I have applied to one great
, B. P. Brent, & he does not believe in young Canaries building worse than old ones.

very perplexing from not knowing what to choose from the load of curious facts on record.— There are two little points, on which I want information, & if you can, which is a mere chance, I think you will not grudge, sometime (for I am in no hurry) giving me information; but if you cannot, then I beg you not to write merely to say that you cannot.
Do you know positively whether chickens or young
scatter & squat when they themselves see large
in air, or perceive danger, or do they do this, only when their mother utters the cry of danger?

Secondly I have been struck with surprise in comparing my memoranda how often crossed animals are said to be very wild, even wilder than either parent: I have thought I would just put a foot-note to this effect, giving my cases: my memory, which I dare not trust, tells me that the cross from wild
was wilder than the wild Boar: do you remember anything of this: I refer to our, memorable visit to
